sections.markdown:
## C — Railroad crossings and the Blue Sign, bicycle lanes, city, rural and secondary roads, interstate driving and vehicle lights (North Carolina)
Knowledge domain: the North Carolina railroad crossing law and safe crossing habits, what to do if stuck on the tracks, the hazards of city, rural and secondary roads, interstate entry, exit and breakdown rules, and the required light standards.

FACT_ID: sec10-F01 | anchor: A01
When the railroad statute's conditions apply, you must stop no more than 50 feet and no less than 15 feet from the nearest rail, and wait until you can cross safely. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0062]

FACT_ID: sec10-F02 | anchor: A01
That stop is required when a visible electric or mechanical signal warns of an approaching train, or when a crossing gate is down or a flagger is signaling a train. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0062]

FACT_ID: sec10-F03 | anchor: A01
The stop is also required when a train within roughly 1500 feet sounds a signal and is an immediate hazard, or when a train is plainly visible and dangerously close. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0062]

FACT_ID: sec10-F04 | anchor: A01
No driver may go through, around or under a crossing gate or barrier while it is closed or moving, and pedestrians may not pass it in any way either. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0062]

FACT_ID: sec10-F05 | anchor: A01
While stopped for a crossing, keep as far right as possible and do not form two lines of traffic unless the road is marked for four or more lanes. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0062]

FACT_ID: sec10-F06 | anchor: A01
Breaking the railroad signal law is an infraction, and an employer who knowingly lets a commercial driver break it also commits an infraction and faces a civil penalty. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0062]

FACT_ID: sec10-F07 | anchor: A01
A yellow and black RR sign warns that a railroad crossing is ahead, so look both ways and listen because you may need to stop. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0062]

FACT_ID: sec10-F08 | anchor: A01
A train always has the right of way, even over police, fire and ambulance vehicles, and if the crossing has a stop sign you must stop fully before crossing. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0062]

FACT_ID: sec10-F09 | anchor: A01
A train going 55 mph needs more than a mile to stop. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0062]

FACT_ID: sec10-F10 | anchor: A02
At a crossing sign, approach carefully, be ready to stop for a train, move on carefully once it passes, and never stop on the tracks for any reason. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0063]

FACT_ID: sec10-F11 | anchor: A02
The crossbuck is the X-shaped sign at the crossing itself, and a smaller sign beneath it shows when there is more than one track. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0063]

FACT_ID: sec10-F12 | anchor: A02
When crossing signals start, you must stop before the gates come down across your side, and moving through a crossing with the gates down is unlawful. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0063]

FACT_ID: sec10-F13 | anchor: A02
Railroads are private property, so driving on or across tracks anywhere other than a designated crossing is illegal. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0063]

FACT_ID: sec10-F14 | anchor: A02
You must always yield to a train, even at a crossing marked only by a crossbuck with no lights or gates. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0063]

FACT_ID: sec10-F15 | anchor: A02
Flashing red lights at a crossbuck mean you stop exactly as you would for any flashing red traffic signal. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0063]

FACT_ID: sec10-F16 | anchor: A02
Do not start moving the moment a train passes, because a second train may be coming either way; wait until the red lights stop flashing. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0063]

FACT_ID: sec10-F17 | anchor: A02
Expect to stop behind vehicles that must stop at crossings, such as school buses, passenger carriers, for-hire vehicles and placarded vehicles hauling explosives or hazardous materials. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0063]

FACT_ID: sec10-F18 | anchor: A02
If the lights start flashing or the gates begin lowering while you are on the tracks, keep moving: do not stop or back up, since the warning allows time to clear. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0063]

FACT_ID: sec10-F19 | anchor: A03
Crossing gates are flexible and cannot trap you, so drive through a gate that comes down beyond you; stopping to back up could stall the car. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0064]

FACT_ID: sec10-F20 | anchor: A03
Gates will not trap you but stopped traffic can, so make sure the traffic ahead will not halt and leave you on the tracks. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0064]

FACT_ID: sec10-F21 | anchor: A03
Every highway-rail crossing in North Carolina must post an Emergency Notification System Blue Sign in each direction showing the crossing ID number, railroad name and an emergency phone number. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0064]

FACT_ID: sec10-F22 | anchor: A03
Using the Blue Sign to call the railroad directly is the fastest way to get a train stopped in an emergency, and each crossing has its own unique USDOT identification number. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0064]

FACT_ID: sec10-F23 | anchor: A03
If your vehicle stalls on or near the tracks, get out right away and walk quickly along the road to a safe spot away from the tracks. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0064]

FACT_ID: sec10-F24 | anchor: A03
Once you are safely away, report the problem using the Blue Sign, and report damaged or missing signs to the Federal Railroad Administration at 1-800-232-0144. [A03]
Why it matters: dynamic fact; phone number can change.
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0064]

FACT_ID: sec10-F25 | anchor: A04
Because bicyclists ride to the right of cars, a cyclist going straight through an intersection is at risk from a motorist turning right. [A04]
Source: [A04 -> pdf-0065]

FACT_ID: sec10-F26 | anchor: A04
If you find you are in the wrong lane for a turn in the city, continue to the next intersection and turn there. [A04]
Source: [A04 -> pdf-0065]

FACT_ID: sec10-F27 | anchor: A04
Avoid riding alongside another car: when the forward car's inside mirror is out of your view, you are likely sitting in its driver's blind spot. [A04]
Source: [A04 -> pdf-0065]

FACT_ID: sec10-F28 | anchor: A04
Do not weave between lanes, and on a one-way street use the center lanes for through travel and the outside lanes for turns. [A04]
Source: [A04 -> pdf-0065]

FACT_ID: sec10-F29 | anchor: A04
Rural roads are often more dangerous than heavy city traffic because they may be narrower, darker and faster. [A04]
Source: [A04 -> pdf-0065]

FACT_ID: sec10-F30 | anchor: A04
Secondary roads tend to have steeper hills, sharper curves and short sight distances, so they cannot be driven safely at speeds suited to primary highways. [A04]
Source: [A04 -> pdf-0065]

FACT_ID: sec10-F31 | anchor: A05
Interstates are safer because opposing traffic is separated, entry and exit points are fewer, and there are no railroad crossings, sharp curves, stop signs or traffic signals. [A05]
Source: [A05 -> pdf-0066]

FACT_ID: sec10-F32 | anchor: A05
When entering an interstate, stay in the acceleration lane until you match the speed of traffic, then merge safely. [A05]
Source: [A05 -> pdf-0066]

FACT_ID: sec10-F33 | anchor: A05
On the interstate keep right and use the left lanes to pass, and avoid tailgating with the two-second rule, since rear-end crashes are among the most frequent there. [A05]
Source: [A05 -> pdf-0066]

FACT_ID: sec10-F34 | anchor: A05
Stop at rest areas often, ideally at least once every 100 miles, and never stop in a travel lane. [A05]
Source: [A05 -> pdf-0066]

FACT_ID: sec10-F35 | anchor: A05
After a breakdown, get well off the road, tie a white cloth to the antenna or left door handle and raise the hood; at night turn on the emergency flashers or parking lights. [A05]
Source: [A05 -> pdf-0066]

FACT_ID: sec10-F36 | anchor: A05
To exit, signal well ahead, move into the deceleration lane without slowing first, and then keep to the posted exit speed. [A05]
Source: [A05 -> pdf-0066]

FACT_ID: sec10-F37 | anchor: A06
On the interstate it is dangerous to drive far below the posted limit; follow the flow of traffic as long as you are not speeding. [A06]
Source: [A06 -> pdf-0067]

FACT_ID: sec10-F38 | anchor: A06
If you miss your exit, do not slow down, back up or turn around; go on to the next exit and find a way back from there. [A06]
Source: [A06 -> pdf-0067]

FACT_ID: sec10-F39 | anchor: A06
If you enter an interstate going the wrong way, pull onto the right shoulder and stop, then turn around when the way is clear; watch for DO NOT ENTER signs to avoid this. [A06]
Source: [A06 -> pdf-0067]

FACT_ID: sec10-F40 | anchor: A06
At night you should be able to see a person 200 feet away with high beams and 75 feet away with low beams. [A06]
Source: [A06 -> pdf-0067]

FACT_ID: sec10-F41 | anchor: A06
Badly aimed headlights glare into the eyes of other road users; vibration can knock them out of line, and a heavily loaded rear can tilt the beams up. [A06]
Source: [A06 -> pdf-0067]

FACT_ID: sec10-F42 | anchor: A06
Taillights must be red and visible from at least 500 feet, and a white light must make the license plate readable from at least 50 feet. [A06]
Source: [A06 -> pdf-0067]

Misconceptions: emergency vehicles do not outrank a train; a crossbuck with no gates still requires yielding; a gate coming down behind or ahead of you will not trap you, so keep moving; once one train passes, another may follow; on an interstate, a missed exit is never fixed by backing up; slowing before the deceleration lane is a mistake.
Mnemonics: slow, look, listen, alert, watch at every crossing; get out and get away, then find the Blue Sign; accelerate on the ramp, decelerate off the road.
Glossary: crossbuck means the X-shaped railroad crossing sign; Blue Sign means the Emergency Notification System sign with the crossing ID and railroad emergency phone; acceleration lane means the entry lane for matching interstate speed; deceleration lane means the exit lane for slowing down; secondary road means a local road not built for highway speeds.
Dynamic facts: emergency and toll phone numbers can change and are flagged as dynamic; confirm on the railroad sign itself or the official website.
